references.text: Earlier in the chapter, Moses warns Pharaoh of the coming locust plague and describes how they will fill the entire land.
The Lord sends a west wind that drives the locusts into the Red Sea, so that not one locust remained in all Egypt.
Moses warns Israel that locusts will devour their crops if they are disobedient to the Lord—a parallel to the plague over Egypt.
The psalmist recalls how God gave the crops to the locusts and the produce of the field to the katydids as part of the plagues over Egypt.
The psalmist describes how God spoke, and locusts came, countless in number, and ate up all growth in their land.
Joel describes a devastating locust plague reminiscent of that in Egypt, where different types of locusts devour everything.
Joel prophesies about a locust plague so great that there has never been its like since ancient days—a description similar to that in Exodus.
The Revelation of John describes locusts coming from the smoke and given power like scorpions, an eschatological echo of the locust plague.
Both verses mark events in Egypt that are historically unique and without parallel, underscoring God's supreme power.
The use of the identical formula about 'something that has never been and will never come' links the swarm of locusts directly to the climax of the tenth plague.
Both verses describe swarms that cover the entire land and complete the destruction of Egypt's resources, showing an escalating judgment.
Uses the identical formula about 'something that has never happened' to mark historical turning points of extreme character, both in God's judgment over Egypt and in Israel's history.
